nameStory: The European rabbit gets its name from its origins in Europe, specifically the Iberian Peninsula of Spain and Portugal. The word 'rabbit' comes from the old French 'rabet,' though these furry hoppers were also called 'coneys' in medieval times. Despite being called European, most rabbits you see today are descendants of domesticated varieties that have either escaped or been released into the wild.
description: The European rabbit is a medium-sized, compact mammal with long ears and powerful hind legs built for hopping. They're smaller than hares, with adults varying widely in size depending on their diet and habitat. Their fur can range from the classic brown-gray 'wild' coloration to spotted, white, black, or mixed patterns - a rainbow of possibilities thanks to centuries of selective breeding. You'll recognize them by their distinctive upright ears, cotton-ball tail, and that characteristic rabbit posture of sitting upright to scan for danger.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded body smaller than a hare with shorter legs relative to body size. When sitting upright in their classic 'loaf' position, they appear almost egg-shaped with their head tucked close to their body.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Soft, dense fur that feels like a plush toy when touched. Colors vary wildly from natural brown-gray to pure white, black, spotted, or mixed patterns - much more variable than native New England mammals.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Lives in groups around extensive burrow systems called warrens. Freezes motionless when threatened, then bolts in a zigzag pattern toward the nearest burrow entrance, unlike hares that rely on speed in open areas.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for multiple round burrow entrances clustered together, often with well-worn paths between them. Their droppings are small, round pellets scattered near feeding areas, and you'll see clean-cut vegetation where they've been nibbling.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four-print hopping pattern with larger hind feet landing ahead of smaller front feet. Tracks often lead directly to burrow entrances rather than wandering widely across the landscape.

habitat: European rabbits prefer open grasslands, meadows, and field edges where they can easily dig their warren systems in well-drained soil. In New England, look for them in parks, golf courses, suburban areas, and agricultural land where the soil isn't too rocky or waterlogged. They need areas with both open feeding grounds and nearby cover for their extensive burrow networks.

seasonality.spring: Most active as breeding season begins, with increased above-ground activity and fresh digging around warren entrances. Young rabbits may be visible near burrow openings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity for feeding and territorial behavior. Warren systems are most extensive, with well-worn paths clearly visible between burrow entrances.
seasonality.fall: Continued activity as they build up fat reserves for winter. Look for increased feeding sign and fresh burrow maintenance.
seasonality.winter: Less active but don't hibernate, emerging from warrens during warmer days. Tracks in snow lead directly between feeding areas and burrow entrances.

funFact: European rabbits are the ancestors of every single domestic rabbit breed in the world - from tiny Netherland Dwarfs to giant Flemish Giants, they all trace back to wild rabbits from Spain and Portugal that were first domesticated by medieval monks.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with native cottontails, but European rabbits are more social (found in groups), live in extensive burrow systems (cottontails use shallow depressions), and show much more color variation. Remember: if you see multiple rabbits near obvious burrow entrances, especially if they're unusual colors, think European rabbit.
contextualKnowledge: There's often confusion about 'wild' rabbits versus escaped domestic rabbits - they're actually the same species! What people call 'wild' European rabbits and pet rabbits are just different varieties of the same animal, like wolves and dogs. Any rabbit you see that's not a native cottontail is likely either an escaped pet or descendant of escaped pets.
compareHints: European rabbits are the only members of their genus, but compared to native cottontails (Sylvilagus species), they're more social, dig extensive burrows instead of using surface nests, and show dramatic color variation. Unlike snowshoe hares, European rabbits don't change color seasonally and prefer to hide in burrows rather than relying on camouflage and speed.
